- **LL-0146.** {D[xi], D[eta]} = D[[xi, eta]] for smooth compactly supported shifts, smooth h and continuous pi, with D[xi] = integral of pi^ij (L_xi h)_ij and the bracket computed with Gateaux derivatives along compactly supported variations (the pi-gradient of D[xi] is L_xi h). Differences, approved by the maintainers (17 November 2026): (a) same setting as the source, (b) partial, (c) convention, (d) and (e) representation (compared with Thiemann, arXiv:gr-qc/0110034, §I.1.1, eqs. (I.1.1.27), (I.1.1.28), (I.1.1.36), (I.1.1.37) (the lecture-note version of the cited book); Hojman-Kuchar-Teitelboim 1976 has not been read): (a) C^infinity data and compactly supported test fields; (b) one global chart R^d, no manifold and no foliation; (c) units 16 pi G = 1 and the kinetic coefficient 1/(d-1) of the Hamiltonian density (1/2 for d = 3), which does not enter this bracket; (d) the momentum constraint in the Lie-derivative form, equal to the ADM form -2 xi_i pi^ij_|j by an integration by parts, formalised as `Lightlike.Canonical.momentumConstraint_eq_adm_of_smooth`; (e) the bracket is defined through pi-gradients and Gateaux derivatives, and the signs of the bracket and of the Lie bracket are fixed by admBracket and lieBracket. The result is partial until the hypersurface version (task F11) replaces the one global chart (b).
- **LL-0147.** {D[xi], H[N]} = H[xi^k d_k N] for smooth compactly supported xi and N, smooth data with positive definite h, with the Hamiltonian density (tr (h pi h pi) - (tr h pi)^2/(d-1))/sqrt(det h) - sqrt(det h) R computed from the coordinate scalar curvature of the geometry API. The proof shows that the scalar curvature is a smooth function of the 2-jet of the metric, that it is covariant under the flow of xi (the library's finite pullback law), that the kinetic term is a scalar density, and differentiates the smeared constraint under the integral sign. Differences, approved by the maintainers (17 November 2026): (a) same setting as the source, (b) partial, (c) convention, (d) and (e) representation (compared with Thiemann, arXiv:gr-qc/0110034, §I.1.1, eqs. (I.1.1.27), (I.1.1.28), (I.1.1.36), (I.1.1.37) (the lecture-note version of the cited book); Hojman-Kuchar-Teitelboim 1976 has not been read): (a) C^infinity data, positive definite h and compactly supported test fields; (b) one global chart R^d, no manifold and no foliation; (c) units 16 pi G = 1 and the kinetic coefficient 1/(d-1) in dimension d (1/2 for d = 3), the one for which the algebra of the constraints closes; (d) the momentum constraint in the Lie-derivative form; (e) the bracket is defined through pi-gradients and Gateaux derivatives, and the signs of the bracket and of the Lie bracket are fixed by admBracket and lieBracket. A grid computation in dimension two (scripts/adm_algebra_check.py) agrees to three digits. The result is partial until the hypersurface version (task F11) replaces the one global chart (b).
- **LL-0152.** For smooth data with positive definite h and symmetric pi and a smooth compactly supported shift xi, the integral of pi^ij (L_xi h)_ij equals the integral of -2 xi_i pi^ij_|j with xi_i = h_ik xi^k and the covariant divergence of Lightlike.christoffel; pointwise the difference is 2 d_j (pi^ij xi_i), and the integral of a derivative of a compactly supported function is zero. The representation difference (d) of the CA1 brackets: approved by the maintainers as representation (17 November 2026). Same setting as the source; one global chart (b) as in the other CA1 results.
- **LL-0153.** {H[N], H[M]} = D[Y] with Y^i = h^ij (N d_j M - M d_j N) for smooth compactly supported N and M, smooth data with positive definite h and symmetric pi, in dimension d at least 2, with the Hamiltonian density (tr (h pi h pi) - (tr h pi)^2/(d-1))/sqrt(det h) - sqrt(det h) R, D[xi] the integral of pi^ij (L_xi h)_ij, and the bracket computed with Gateaux derivatives along compactly supported variations. The proof differentiates the first-order form of H[N] along M times the pi-gradient of H[M], antisymmetrizes, and reduces the remaining coefficient to -2 times the covariant divergence of pi by an index computation with the Christoffel symbols; the ADM form of the momentum constraint closes the argument. Compared with Thiemann, arXiv:gr-qc/0110034, sec. I.1.1, eq. (I.1.1.37) (the lecture-note version of the cited book), same signs and structure function; Hojman-Kuchar-Teitelboim 1976 has not been read. Differences, approved by the maintainers (17 November 2026): (a) same setting as the source; (b) partial: one global chart R^d, no manifold and no foliation (task F11); (c) convention: units 16 pi G = 1 and the kinetic coefficient 1/(d-1); (d) representation: D[xi] in the Lie-derivative form, equal to the ADM form by Lightlike.Canonical.momentumConstraint_eq_adm_of_smooth; (e) representation: the bracket through pi-gradients and Gateaux derivatives. The result is partial until the hypersurface version (task F11) replaces the one global chart (b).

Notes:

- **LL-0163.** For a strongly continuous one-parameter group of unitaries U(t) on a complex Hilbert space, the generator A psi = -i d/dt U(t) psi at t = 0, on the vectors where the derivative exists, is self-adjoint: A is contained in its adjoint and its adjoint in A. This is one direction of Stone's theorem; the converse, that every self-adjoint operator generates such a group, is the task T-OP1-P2. Compared with Moretti, Theorem 142, p. 83 (read): (a) there is a unique self-adjoint generator A with U(t) = exp(-itA), (b) A psi = i lim (U(t) - 1) psi / t on the vectors where the limit exists; also with Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics (AMS online edition), Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, pp. 123-124 (read). The Hall chapters are cited but were not read. Difference to be approved by a maintainer (convention): the library's generator is -i d/dt U(t) at 0, with U(t) = exp(itA), the negative of Moretti's (U(t) = exp(-itA)).
- **LL-0164.** On a complex Hilbert space, a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group is determined by its generator: if U and V have the same generator then U(t) = V(t) for all t. This is the uniqueness part of Stone's theorem. Compared with Moretti, Theorem 142, p. 83 (read): (a) there is a unique self-adjoint generator A with U(t) = exp(-itA), (b) A psi = i lim (U(t) - 1) psi / t on the vectors where the limit exists; also with Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics (AMS online edition), Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, pp. 123-124 (read). The Hall chapters are cited but were not read. Difference to be approved by a maintainer (convention): the library's generator is -i d/dt U(t) at 0, with U(t) = exp(itA), the negative of Moretti's (U(t) = exp(-itA)).
- **LL-0165.** For the translation group (U(t) psi)(x) = psi(x + t) on L^2(R) and psi in the domain of its generator, there are smooth compactly supported functions psi_n with psi_n -> psi and psi_n' -> i A psi in L^2, where A is the generator: C_c^infinity is a core, and the generator is the momentum operator -i d/dx. The comparison with the cited source is pending: the registry location is the chapter, and the statement was not read there. Difference to be approved by a maintainer: the core property is stated through approximating sequences, not as the equality of the closure of the restriction with the generator.
- **LL-0166.** The operator -i d/dx on the C^2 functions supported inside (0, 1) is densely defined in L^2(0, 1), and its deficiency spaces at i and -i are one-dimensional, so it has self-adjoint extensions and none is distinguished. The comparison with the cited source is pending: the registry location is the chapter, and the statement was not read there. Difference to be approved by a maintainer: the domain is the C^2 functions supported inside (0, 1); the closure of the operator is the same from C_c^infinity (the closure of the momentum graph on the interval).
- **LL-0167.** In L^2(0, 1) x L^2(0, 1), the closure of the graph of -i d/dx on C_c^infinity(0, 1) equals the closure of its graph on the C^2 functions supported inside (0, 1). The proof mollifies. The comparison with the cited source is pending: the registry location is the chapter, and the statement was not read there.
- **LL-0168.** For a complex inner product space h, fockRepOf h is a Fock representation: Weyl unitaries W(f) satisfying the Weyl relations, with a unit vector Omega that is cyclic for them and has <Omega, W(f) Omega> = exp(-|f|^2 / 4). The Hilbert space is the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the Fock kernel (Mathlib's RKHS.OfKernel). The representation difference is approved by the maintainers (18 November 2026): a Fock representation is characterised by its cyclic vacuum and vacuum expectation, not built on the symmetric Fock space; any two such representations are unitarily equivalent (uniqueness of the Fock representation). The comparison with the cited source is pending: the registry location is the chapter, and the statement was not read there.
- **LL-0169.** For two Fock representations R on K1 and S on K2 (complete) of the same complex inner product space, the unitary fockUnitary R S from K1 onto K2 maps the vacuum to the vacuum and intertwines the Weyl unitaries. The map W(f) Omega to W(f) Omega' is well defined and norm preserving on the dense span of these vectors and extends to a unitary. The representation difference of the existence of a Fock representation is approved by the maintainers (18 November 2026). The comparison with the cited source is pending: the registry location is the chapter, and the statement was not read there.
- **LL-0183.** On Matrix n n C with tau^{-i beta}(B) = e^{beta H} B e^{-beta H}: a matrix rho of trace 1 satisfies tr(rho A B) = tr(rho tau^{-i beta}(B) A) for all A, B (the beta-KMS condition, eq. (2.24)) iff rho = e^{-beta H} / tr e^{-beta H}. Compared with Jaksic-Ogata-Pautrat-Pillet, Section 2.9, eq. (2.24) and Proposition 2.20, p. 53 (read). The statement is more general than the source's: H is any matrix with tr e^{-beta H} != 0 (the source takes H self-adjoint, where this holds), and rho is only required to have trace 1 (the source's states are positive).
- **LL-0184.** For the momentum P = -i d/dx on L^2(0, 1): the domain of the adjoint is D_max, the functions absolutely continuous on [0, 1] with derivative in L^2 (mem_adjoint_iff_ac, in MomentumBoundary.lean); the closed operator P is the adjoint on D_0 = {psi in D_max : psi(0) = psi(1) = 0} and equals the closure of -i d/dx on the C^2 functions supported inside (0, 1) (momentumZero_eq_closure); a self-adjoint operator B extends P iff B = P_theta, the adjoint on D_theta = {psi in D_max : psi(1) = e^{i theta} psi(0)}, for some real theta. Compared with Bonneau-Faraut-Valent, Section 5.3, eq. (14), p. 8, and Appendix A.3, p. 19 (read). Differences, kind convention, to be approved by a maintainer: (a) the interval is [0, 1] (L = 1); (b) theta ranges over the reals instead of [0, 2 pi] (the same operators).
- **LL-0185.** For P_theta = -i d/dx on D_theta = {psi in D_max(0, 1) : psi(1) = e^{i theta} psi(0)}: the plane waves e^{i(theta + 2 pi n)x}, n in Z, lie in D_theta, are eigenvectors with eigenvalue theta + 2 pi n and are orthonormal; every eigenvalue is of this form and every eigenvector is a multiple of the plane wave; the spectrum in Physlib's sense (LinearPMap.spectrum: z is in the resolvent set iff P_theta - z is a bijection of the domain onto L^2(0, 1) with continuous inverse) is theta + 2 pi Z and equals the point spectrum. The resolvent equation is solved explicitly off theta + 2 pi Z. Compared with Bonneau-Faraut-Valent, Section 5.3, p. 8, eq. (15) and the sentence before it ('the spectra are purely discrete') (read). Differences, kind convention, to be approved by a maintainer: hbar = 1, L = 1, and the eigenvalue 2 pi hbar nu / L, nu = n + theta / 2 pi, is written theta + 2 pi n.
- **LL-0194.** Compared with Bar-Ginoux-Pfaffle, Definition 4.2.1, p. 116 and Proposition 4.2.3 (1), (4), pp. 117-119 (read). A Weyl system is a map W from a real symplectic vector space into a unital star algebra over C with W(0) = 1, W(-phi) = W(phi)* and the Weyl relation.
- **LL-0195.** Compared with Bar-Ginoux-Pfaffle, Example 4.2.2, pp. 116-117 (read): CCR(V, omega) is the C*-subalgebra of L(l2(V)) generated by (W(phi)F)(psi) = exp(i omega(phi, psi)/2) F(phi + psi); here l2(V) is any Hilbert space with a Hilbert basis indexed by V. Uniqueness up to *-isomorphism (Theorem 4.2.9) is not stated.
- **LL-0196.** Compared with Derezinski, Theorem 10, p. 17, and the definitions of Section 4.1, pp. 14-15 (read). The tensor product of C^2 x ... x C^2 with K is represented as L^2(configurations; K) (PiLp 2), on which B x 1_K acts by (B x 1) f x = sum_y B x y f y (tensorOne) and I_n x T by sum_y I_n x y T (f y) (tensorOp); K is given explicitly, the vacuum space (the joint kernel of the annihilation operators a_j = (phi_{2j} + i phi_{2j+1})/2), which is closed, so a Hilbert space when H is; H may be any complex inner product space, with symmetric phi_b (self-adjoint on a Hilbert space, isCAROn_iff); indices are 0-based. Irreducibility is the definition of p. 15, and 'irreducible iff K = C' is proved for H nonzero: as printed, the source's equivalence fails at H = {0}, which is irreducible by the p. 15 definition while K = {0}. In part 2, K_+ + K_- with 1 + (-1) is represented by K with the self-adjoint unitary T, whose eigenspaces ker(T - 1) and ker(T + 1) are orthogonal and span K (involution_decomposition).
- **LL-0197.** Compared with Derezinski, Corollary 2, p. 17 (read): a representation over a 2n-dimensional real Hilbert space Y is the family phi_i = phi(y_i) on an orthonormal basis y_1, ..., y_2n (the source's identification, p. 14), i.e. a representation over R^{2n}; stated for nonzero spaces, as in LL-0196.
- **LL-0198.** Compared with Derezinski, Theorem 4, p. 12 (statement) and Faulhuber, Section 7.3.1, pp. 90-94 (von Neumann's proof), read. The symplectic space is a finite-dimensional complex inner product space h with sigma = Im<.,.> (the repository's CCRRep, regular by definition); the reference representation is the repository's Fock representation fockRepOf h (cyclic vacuum with <Omega, W f Omega> = exp(-|f|^2/4)), not the Schrodinger representation on L^2(X), to which it is unitarily equivalent by the Bargmann transform (not formalized); L^2(X) tensor K is the Hilbert sum over an orthonormal basis of the range of the Gaussian projection P0 = (2 pi)^{-d} int exp(-|z|^2/4) W z dz of the closed invariant subspaces generated by the basis vectors, each a Fock representation. 'Irreducible iff K = C' is proved for nonzero spaces (as printed it fails for H = {0}, irreducible by the p. 10 definition).
- **LL-0199.** Compared with Derezinski, Corollary 1, p. 12, and Faulhuber, Theorem 7.32, pp. 90-94 (read): with the same representation of the symplectic space and of the reference representation as LL-0198, for nonzero spaces.
- **LL-0200.** Compared with Derezinski, Section 9.1, p. 38 and Section 3.1, pp. 9-10 (read). The symplectic space is a complex inner product space h with sigma = Im<.,.>; a quasi-free vector satisfies <Psi, W y Psi> = exp(-eta(y, y)/4) for a symmetric real bilinear form eta (the source's quadratic form y eta y).
- **LL-0201.** Compared with Derezinski, Theorem 39 (1), p. 39 (read). The field operator phi(y) is the generator of t -> W(t y) = exp(i t phi(y)); (Psi | phi(y1) phi(y2) Psi) is read as (phi(y1) Psi | phi(y2) Psi); eta is the symmetric real bilinear form of (70) and sigma = Im<.,.> is the source's omega. The corrected formula (eta + i sigma)/2 is stated. Source error: as printed, Theorem 39 (1) reads y1 (eta + 2 i omega) y2; the second-order expansion of (70) gives (eta + i omega)/2, which the Fock vacuum (eta = Re<.,.>, two-point function <f, g>/2, FockRep.inner_field_field_vacuum) confirms.
- **LL-0202.** Compared with Derezinski, Theorem 39 (2), p. 39 (read): abs_symp_le_two_mul is the printed bound with the constant 2; abs_symp_le has the constant 1.
- **LL-0203.** Compared with Derezinski, Section 7.1, p. 29 and Section 5.3, p. 20 (read). The antisymmetric Fock space of Z is represented as a Hilbert space with a Hilbert basis indexed by the finite subsets of ι, for a Hilbert basis (e_i) of Z indexed by a linearly ordered ι (the basis vector of a finite set S stands for the normalized wedge product of the e_i, i in S, in increasing order; l^2(Finset ι) is one such space); the identification with the antisymmetric tensors is not built. Y = Re(Z + conj Z) with (z, conj z) α (w, conj w) = Re<z, w> is written as Z with the real scalar product Re<.,.>.
- **LL-0204.** Compared with Derezinski, Section 5.2, Theorem 13, p. 19 and Section 5.5, p. 21 (read). The Fock space is the repository's Fock representation (a cyclic vacuum with <Omega, W f Omega> = exp(-|f|^2/4)), the symmetric Fock space of Section 5.5; Gamma(p) is characterized by Gamma(p) W(f) Omega = exp((|p f|^2 - |f|^2)/4) W(p f) Omega, i.e. Gamma(p) e(f) = e(p f) on the exponential vectors e(f) = exp(|f|^2/4) W(f) Omega, not by p tensor n on the n-particle spaces (not built). Boundedness: a bounded operator with this action exists iff |p| <= 1.
- **LL-0205.** Compared with Derezinski, Section 6.4, Theorem 24, p. 27 (read), for a unitary r of Z (p = r, c = d = 0 in (46), so U_r^j = Gamma(r)); the general r in Sp_2(Y) is Shale's theorem, in the repository's Shale files. Uniqueness up to a phase from the triviality of the commutant of the Fock representation (commutant_scalar).
- **LL-0206.** Compared with Panangaden, arXiv:2110.01678, Proposition 5.4 (p. 43, Gibbs implies KMS whenever the Gibbs state exists), Remark 5.1, Definition 5.8 (p. 46) and Proposition 5.9 (p. 47) (read). H is the self-adjoint operator of a Hilbert basis b and real eigenvalues ev with sum of e^{-beta ev_n} finite, on its natural domain; every H with trace-class e^{-beta H} has this form (e^{-beta H} is compact and self-adjoint; Teschl, Theorem 6.6). The Gibbs state is the trace of e^{-beta H} A in the eigenbasis over Z; e^{itH} is the diagonal unitary diag(e^{it ev_n}).
- **LL-0207.** Compared with Landsman, arXiv:math-ph/9807030, Definition 2.8.1 (p. 35, states), Definition 2.12.1 (p. 44), Proposition 2.12.8 and Theorem 2.12.9 with its proof (p. 46) (read). Stated for compact X (the source reduces C_0(X) to this case); a state is a linear functional on C(X, C) that is nonnegative on pointwise nonnegative functions with value 1 at 1 (in C(X) the positive elements are the pointwise nonnegative functions); the homeomorphism of Theorem 2.12.9 is Mathlib's WeakDual.CharacterSpace.homeoEval once pure states are the characters.
- **LL-0208.** Compared with Landsman, arXiv:math-ph/9807030, Theorem 2.12.9 and its proof (p. 46, read): the reduction of C_0(X) to C of the one-point compactification. A state of C_0(X) is a positive linear functional with supremum 1 over the [0, 1]-valued functions (Definition 2.8.6, p. 36: positive with norm 1; for a positive functional the norm is this supremum); the extension is Proposition 2.8.7, p. 37; it extends to the state F -> omega(F - F(infinity)) + F(infinity), a pure state to a pure one, and the point at infinity is excluded since a state is nonzero.
- **LL-0209.** Compared with Huang, Wang, Wu, Meng, arXiv:2610.21070, Section 3.2.1, p. 5 (read): Pi(nu, eta) the probability couplings, W_1 the infimum of the cost of d, and the easy direction of (KR) for unit Lipschitz u. The equality (KR) is the next entry.
- **LL-0210.** Compared with Huang, Wang, Wu, Meng, arXiv:2610.21070, Section 8.1, (8.1), p. 46 (read): the finite transport problem, min over couplings of the cost equals max over a_i + b_j <= d(x_i, x_j) of the dual value, with a minimum attained. Here the duality is for every continuous cost on a compact metric space, with an optimal coupling; the proof goes through the Hahn-Banach theorem and the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem.
- **LL-0211.** Compared with Huang, Wang, Wu, Meng, arXiv:2610.21070, Section 3.2.1, p. 5, (KR) (read): on a compact metric space, for Borel probability measures, inf over couplings of the integral of d equals sup over unit Lipschitz u of the pairing with nu - eta; Section 3.7 (1), p. 16: the minimum distance-cost coupling; Section 8.1, (8.2), p. 46: the c-transform u_i = min_j (d(x_i, x_j) - b_j), applied here on the space instead of on a finite net.
- **LL-0220.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.2, Theorem 6.6, p. 136 (read, online edition). Stated for a compact symmetric operator on a real or complex Hilbert space. The expansion (6.5), K = sum over the spectrum of lambda P_K({lambda}), is stated in a Hilbert basis of eigenvectors; grouping the basis vectors by eigenvalue gives the projections P_K({lambda}). The spectrum is stated as countable, its nonzero points as eigenvalues (read literally, 'the spectrum consists of eigenvalues' fails at 0: diag(1/(n+1)) on l2(N) is compact and self-adjoint with 0 in its spectrum and 0 not an eigenvalue, invDiag_zero_mem_spectrum_not_hasEigenvalue), and the eigenvalues of norm at least epsilon as finitely many. Hilbert-Schmidt operators are compact (Teschl, Section 6.3, p. 139), isCompactOperator_of_isHilbertSchmidt.
- **LL-0233.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.2, Theorem 6.7 and (6.7), p. 137 (read, online edition), for a compact operator on a real or complex Hilbert space. The orthonormal sets are families indexed by a type and the series (6.6) are stated pointwise; 'finitely many singular values or they converge to zero' is stated as finitely many s_j >= epsilon for every epsilon > 0; for every mu != 0 the mu-eigenspace of K*K (of KK*) is the span of the phi_j (the phi'_j) with s_j^2 = mu, of dimension #{j | s_j^2 = mu}; (6.7) is stated as an upper bound attained for K != 0 (for K = 0 there are no singular values).
- **LL-0234.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.3, (6.19)-(6.23) and Lemma 6.12, pp. 141-142 (read, online edition). schattenSum p K is the supremum (6.23) to the power p, over pairs of finite orthonormal families; for every canonical form and p >= 1 it equals the sum of s_j^p (6.19), so that sum does not depend on the canonical form. (6.21) and (6.22) are stated for schattenSum.
- **LL-0235.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.3, Lemma 6.10, (6.14)-(6.17), p. 140, and p. 142 (read, online edition). The repository's Hilbert-Schmidt class (square sum finite in one Hilbert basis) is J_2: compact with finite schattenSum 2.
- **LL-0236.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.3, p. 142 and Lemma 6.13, (6.24), pp. 142-143 (read, online edition). The repository's trace class (diagonal sums of |K| finite in one Hilbert basis) is J_1: compact with finite schattenSum 1; (6.24) is stated with the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of K_1* (equal to that of K_1).
- **LL-0237.** Compared with Teschl, Section 6.3, Lemma 6.12, pp. 141-142 (read, online edition). 'J_p(H) with the norm is a Banach space' is stated as the norm properties (triangle inequality, homogeneity, definiteness) and completeness of the Cauchy sequences of compact operators with finite norm; no normed-space instance on J_p is built.
- **LL-0258.** Compared with Dereziński, arXiv:math-ph/0511030, Theorem 13 (1), p. 19 ([dΓ(h1), dΓ(h2)] = dΓ([h1, h2])) and Theorem 18 (2), (4), p. 22 ([dΓ(h), a(w)] = -a(h* w), [dΓ(h), a*(w)] = a*(hw)) (read). Here Z = ℂⁿ and dΓ(h) = ∑ h_ij a_i* a_j in any algebra over ℂ whose a_i, a_i* satisfy the CAR or the CCR.
- **LL-0259.** Compared with Dereziński, arXiv:math-ph/0511030, Theorem 13 (1), p. 19 and Theorem 18 (2), (4), p. 22 (read). Here Z is any complex inner product space, a* is linear and a antilinear on Z with the CAR or the CCR in an algebra over ℂ, and h = ∑ₖ |uₖ⟩⟨vₖ| has finite rank, where the source allows every h ∈ B(Z).
- **LL-0265.** Compared with Bär-Ginoux-Pfäffle, arXiv:0806.1036, Proposition 4.2.3 (2), (3), pp. 117-118 (read): ‖W(φ) - W(ψ)‖ = 2 for φ ≠ ψ, and the algebra A of a Weyl system (A, W) is not separable unless V = {0}; here A is any nontrivial C*-algebra, and the CCR algebra of Example 4.2.2 is the case ccrAlgebra_not_separableSpace.
- **LL-0266.** Compared with Dereziński, arXiv:math-ph/0511030, Theorem 18 (2), (4), p. 22 ([dΓ(h), a(w)] = -a(h* w), [dΓ(h), a*(w)] = a*(hw), in the bosonic and the fermionic case) and Theorem 13 (1), p. 19 ([dΓ(h₁), dΓ(h₂)] = dΓ([h₁, h₂])), with Γⁿ_{s/a}(Z) = Θⁿ_{s/a} ⊗ⁿZ (Section 5.3, p. 20), dΓₙ(h) = ∑ⱼ 1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ h ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ 1 (Section 5.2, p. 19), a*(w)Ψ = √(n+1) Θ_{s/a}(w ⊗ Ψ) and a(w) = a*(w)* (Section 5.7, p. 22) (read). Here ⊗ⁿZ is the coordinate tensor power ℓ²(Fin n → ι) of a Hilbert basis of Z, and the identities hold between consecutive tensor powers, sector by sector.
- **LL-0272.** For a positive definite rho of trace 1, rho is KMS for the dynamics generated by H = log rho at beta = -1: tr(rho A B) = tr(rho tau^{-i beta}(B) A) with tau^{-i beta}(B) = e^{beta H} B e^{-beta H}, so tr(rho A B) = tr(rho e^{-log rho} B e^{log rho} A). Sign convention: the Gibbs state e^{-beta H}/tr e^{-beta H} at beta = -1 and H = log rho is rho itself, which is why the modular Hamiltonian is log rho and beta is -1 (the entanglement Hamiltonian -log rho has beta = 1). Compared with Jaksic-Ogata-Pautrat-Pillet, arXiv:1106.3786, Section 2.12.1, pp. 62-63 (read): the modular dynamics varsigma_rho^t(A) = e^{it log rho} A e^{-it log rho} and the (beta = -1)-KMS property of rho; the same sign and the same generator. log rho is built from the spectral decomposition (logPosDef, exp_logPosDef); the proof is isKMS_iff_eq_gibbs (LL-0183) with e^{log rho} = rho.

Notes:

- **LL-0214.** Compared with Paschke and Sitarz, arXiv:q-alg/9612029, Lemma 1 (p. 2), Lemma 3 (p. 3, the first half), Lemma 4 (p. 3) and Lemma 6 (p. 5), and Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.2 (pp. 12-13) (read), for a family of central self-adjoint orthogonal projections P_i of a finite-dimensional real star-algebra with sum 1.
- **LL-0215.** Compared with Paschke and Sitarz, arXiv:q-alg/9612029, Section 2 (complex spectral triples) and Lemma 2 (pp. 2-3) (read): for A = ⊕ M_(n_i)(C) represented complex-linearly, H_ij ≅ C^(n_i) ⊗ C^(r_ij) ⊗ C^(n_j) with a acting as a_i on the first factor and J π(b*) J as right multiplication by b_j on the last.
- **LL-0216.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.2, p. 12 (read): K(H_ij) = H_ji, so the matrix of multiplicities is symmetric, m_ij = m_ji; here for A = ⊕ M_(n_i)(C) represented complex-linearly, with r_ij the multiplicity in H_ij ≅ C^(n_i) ⊗ C^(r_ij) ⊗ C^(n_j).
- **LL-0217.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.2, p. 13 (read): conversely, if the matrix of multiplicities is symmetric it is possible to define J, J (e_a ⊗ ψ ⊗ e_b) = e_b ⊗ ψ̄ ⊗ e_a; and Section 3.3, p. 13: the chirality is ±1 on H_ij with χ_ij = χ_ji. Here A = ⊕ M_(n_i)(C), r symmetric with every summand acting on some vertex (faithfulness), D = 0.
- **LL-0218.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.2, p. 13 (read): if the matrix of multiplicities is symmetric, the charge conjugation is unique up to unitary equivalence and acts as J (e_a ⊗ ψ ⊗ e_b) = e_b ⊗ ψ̄ ⊗ e_a; the orthonormal basis with L_ii ψ = ψ is exists_orthonormalBasis_fixed. Here A = ⊕ M_(n_i)(C) represented complex-linearly; the unitary intertwines π and J with the model krajewskiReal of the multiplicity matrix.
- **LL-0219.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.4, p. 15 (read): D = D_L + D_R with [D_L, π(A)] = [D_R, J π(A) J⁻¹] = 0, unique since D anticommutes with χ, D_L = J D_R J⁻¹, so D = Δ + J Δ J⁻¹ with Δ hermitian, commuting with J π(A) J⁻¹ and anticommuting with χ; and Paschke-Sitarz, arXiv:q-alg/9612029, Lemma 6, p. 5 (the second half). The chirality is assumed scalar on each vertex H_ij, which Paschke-Sitarz Lemma 3 (p. 3) derives from the Hochschild-cycle axiom.
- **LL-0254.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 2, p. 2 (A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(K), K = ℝ, ℂ, ℍ) and Section 3.1, p. 10 (read): 'Mₙ(ℝ) and Mₙ(ℍ) have only one irreducible representation, the fundamental one ... all our formulae remain valid, provided the indices i and j label irreducible representations of A'. Here A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℝ): π extends to the complex-linear σ(x) = π(Re x) + i π(Im x) of ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℂ), J is a real structure for it, and the uniqueness theorem for complex summands gives the unitary. Mₙ(ℍ) summands, Mₙ(ℂ) summands acting real-linearly, mixed algebras and the sign conditions of Table 1, p. 14 are not covered.
- **LL-0255.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.1, p. 10 (read): 'all our formulae remain valid, provided the indices i and j label irreducible representations of A'. Here the irreducible representations are given by a complexification (σ, φ) of the triple; the order-zero and first-order conditions pass from π(A) to its complex span, and the uniqueness theorem for complex summands applies to σ. The complexification is an input; for A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℝ) it is constructed in RealSummands.lean.
- **LL-0256.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.1, p. 10 (read): 'Mₙ(ℝ) and Mₙ(ℍ) have only one irreducible representation, the fundamental one ... Hᵢⱼ is isomorphic to ℂⁿⁱ ⊗ ℂᵐⁱʲ ⊗ ℂⁿʲ, where nᵢ is the dimension of the irreducible representation i', which for Mₙ(ℍ) is 2n. Here A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℍ): with ρ_αβ(q) = π(E_αβ(q)) and the identification ℍ ⊗_ℝ ℂ ≅ M₂(ℂ), q ↦ [[a + b i, c + d i], [-c + d i, a - b i]], the operators (ρ_αβ)_ℂ(E_st) are matrix units of ⊕ M₂ₙᵢ(ℂ) on H, and φ(a)_{(αs)(βt)} = ι(a_αβ)_st gives π = σ ∘ φ. Mixed algebras and the sign conditions of Table 1, p. 14 are not covered.
- **LL-0257.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.1, p. 10 (read): 'Mₙ(ℂ) has two inequivalent irreducible representations, the fundamental one and its complex conjugate. However, all our formulae remain valid, provided the indices i and j label irreducible representations of A'. Here A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℂ) with a real-linear π: Q± = (1 ∓ i π(i·1))/2 split H into the parts where π is complex-linear (fundamental) and antilinear (conjugate); the units Q± π(E^i_αβ) of the blocks (i, ±) that occur (Q± π(1ᵢ) ≠ 0) and φ(a) = (aᵢ, āᵢ) give the complexification. The index set of the model is the set of representations (i, ±) that occur. Mixed algebras and the sign conditions of Table 1, p. 14 are not covered.
- **LL-0260.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 2, p. 2 (A = ⊕ Mₙᵢ(K), K = ℝ, ℂ, ℍ) and Section 3.1, p. 10 (read): 'Mₙ(ℝ) and Mₙ(ℍ) have only one irreducible representation, the fundamental one, whereas Mₙ(ℂ) has two inequivalent irreducible representations, the fundamental one and its complex conjugate. However, all our formulae remain valid, provided the indices i and j label irreducible representations of A'. Here A = ⊕ Mₙ(ℝ) × ⊕ Mₙ(ℂ) × ⊕ Mₙ(ℍ) with a real-linear π: the restrictions of π to the three factors give units ψ₁(E^i_αβ), ψ±(E^i_αβ) (ψ±(Y) = ½(ψ₂(Y) ∓ i ψ₂(iY)), over the representations (i, ±) that occur) and the quaternionic units of M₂ₙ(ℂ); together they are one system of matrix units, and the uniqueness theorem for complex summands gives the unitary onto the model indexed by the irreducible representations that occur. The sign conditions of Table 1, p. 14 (the S⁰-real structure and the intersection form) are not covered.
- **LL-0262.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.3, p. 13 (read): 'Since χ = Σ_p π(x^p) J π(y^p) J⁻¹, with x^p, y^p ∈ A, χᵢⱼ is scalar matrix. Furthermore χᵢⱼ = ±1 as follows from χ² = 1. We also have [χ, J] = 0 so that χᵢⱼ = χⱼᵢ.' Here for a complex-linear triple over ⊕ Mₙᵢ(ℂ) and an orientable grading γ = Σ_p π(x_p) J π(y_p) J: γ acts on the multiplicity space Vᵢⱼ as cᵢⱼ = Σ_p (x_p)ᵢ₀₀ conj((y_p)ⱼ₀₀), cᵢⱼ = ±1 on a nonzero vertex and cⱼᵢ = cᵢⱼ.
- **LL-0263.** Compared with Krajewski, arXiv:hep-th/9701081, Section 3.3, p. 14 and Table 1 (read): 'In the real case, it is still given by a symmetric matrix with entries in Z whose indices label irreducibles representations of A. However, it is no longer the intersection form and the signs of its entries satisfy additional requirements that are summarized ... in table 1': μ_{iαj} μ_{iᾱj} ≥ 0 and μ_{iαjβ} μ_{iᾱjβ̄} ≥ 0. Here μ_kl = Re(c_kl) r_kl on the complexified model of a mixed algebra ⊕ Mₙ(ℝ) × ⊕ Mₙ(ℂ) × ⊕ Mₙ(ℍ) with an orientable grading; the conditions are stated for both representations of a complex summand that occur. The intersection form ∩ᵢⱼ = Tr(χ π(pᵢ) J π(pⱼ) J⁻¹) of minimal projections pᵢ, pⱼ is every entry of Table 1: μ, Σ_α μ, 2μ (real against real, complex, quaternionic), Σ_αβ μ, 2 Σ_α μ (complex against complex, quaternionic) and 4μ (quaternionic against quaternionic), where μ_kl = c_kl r_kl with c_kl the scalar of the chirality on the vertex.

## Field theory in finite dimensions

API map: [Lightlike/FieldTheory/API-map.md](../Lightlike/FieldTheory/API-map.md)

| ID | Result | Status | Tier | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LL-0268 | The Brydges–Kennedy Taylor forest formula, H(1) as the sum over forests F of the integrals over the unit cube of F of the F-th partial derivative of H at X^F(h), for smooth H from R^{P_n} to a Banach space (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.FieldTheory.Forest.forest_formula_restrict`, `Lightlike.FieldTheory.Forest.forest_formula`, `Lightlike.FieldTheory.Forest.forestPoint_eq_path_inf` in [Formula.lean](../Lightlike/FieldTheory/Forest/Formula.lean) |
| LL-0269 | The forest matrix, with 1 on the diagonal and the infimum of the parameters along the paths of F off it, is positive semidefinite for parameters at most 1 (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.FieldTheory.Forest.forestMatrix`, `Lightlike.FieldTheory.Forest.posSemidef_forestMatrix` in [Positivity.lean](../Lightlike/FieldTheory/Forest/Positivity.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-0268.** Compared with Abdesselam and Rivasseau, arXiv:hep-th/9409094, Theorem III.1, eq. (III.2), p. 13, and the definition of h^F_l on p. 3 (read): for H in the space of smooth functions from R^{P_n} to a Banach space V, H(1) is the sum over the forests F of the integrals over the h_l in the unit interval, l in F, of the product over l in F of the partial derivatives in x_l of H at X^F(h), whose entry at the link l is the infimum of the h along the unique path of F joining the ends of l, and 0 if there is none. forest_formula_restrict is this statement for H : (Link n -> R) -> V with ContDiff R infinity H and V a real Banach space; forest_formula states it with the integral over the whole cube of R^{P_n} of the same integrand, a function of the h_l, l in F, only. Differences from the cited theorem, all representation, with the meaning unchanged: the points 1, ..., n are Fin n and P_n is Link n, the unordered pairs s(a, b) with a /= b; X^F(h)_l is defined by the ultrametric of F (the largest h_m, m in F, such that the ends of l are joined by the links of F with parameter at least h_m, 0 if none), which for h >= 0, in particular on the unit cube, is the infimum along the path of F and 0 if there is no path (forestPoint_eq_path_inf, forestPoint_of_not_linked); the integral over the unit cube of F is the integral over F -> R for the product of the uniform measures on the unit interval, h extended by 0 off F, which does not change X^F(h) (forestPoint_congr); the product of the partial derivatives is the iterated Frechet partial derivative pdF along the coordinate vectors, independent of the order (pd_comm, pdF_insert). Proof: not the source's (the algebraic formula (II.1) for polynomials and density in S, pp. 13-14), but the iterated Taylor interpolation of Gurau, Rivasseau and Sfondrini, arXiv:1401.5003, Theorem 6.1, eq. (6.1), p. 107, and its proof, pp. 107-109 (read), as an induction on the number of links in which the new link is the one with the smallest parameter (T_succ, interp_insert_update); ties have measure zero (cube_eq_null).
- **LL-0269.** Compared with Rivasseau and Wang, arXiv:1003.1037, Theorem II.1, eq. (II-1), p. 2, and the convex combination (II-4) of block matrices of ones, pp. 2-3 (read): the symmetric n x n matrix X^F with X_ii = 1 and X_ij the infimum of the parameters w on the path of the forest F from i to j (0 if there is none) is positive. posSemidef_forestMatrix: for any finite set of links F and parameters with w_l <= 1 on F, forestMatrix F w (1 on the diagonal, the ultrametric of F off it, equal to the path infimum for w >= 0 by forestPoint_eq_path_inf and forestMatrix_eq_forestPoint) is Matrix.PosSemidef. Difference, representation, with the meaning unchanged: positive is Matrix.PosSemidef (symmetric with x^T X x >= 0); the matrix can be singular (one link with parameter 1 gives the 2 x 2 matrix of ones), so the source's positive is positive semidefinite. Not a difference: the statement holds for any finite set of links and needs only w_l <= 1 on F, which contains the source's case of a forest with parameters in the unit interval. Proof: the integral form of (II-4): for t in (0, 1], t <= X_ij exactly when i and j are joined by the links with w >= t (le_ultra_iff), so X is the integral over t of the block matrices of ones of those clusters, each positive (sum_block_nonneg).
